extracted.intended_audience: general readers, film students, and researchers interested in The War Game or British television/film history
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia encyclopedia entry summarising the 1965 British pseudo-documentary The War Game: synopsis, style, production, release, reception, and legacy. Useful for readers seeking an overview of the film's content, techniques, controversies, and critical reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story told in the style of a news magazine programme
rubrics_metrics.description: The story is told in the style of a news magazine programme. It wavers between a pseudo-documentary and a drama film, with characters acknowledging the presence of the camera in some segments and others filmed as if the camera was not present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the hybrid format: alternation of strands (documentary-style chronology, reportage-like images, contemporary interviews, optimistic commentary, fictional interviews). The combination also qualifies it as a mondo film; the format supports a plausibility/realism effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of voice-over narration to argue a point
rubrics_metrics.description: The film has a voice-over narration that describes the events depicted as plausible occurrences during and after a nuclear war. The narrator seeks to convince the viewing audience that the civil defence policies of 1965 have not realistically prepared the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narration functions didactically to critique policy (e.g., neglect of panic buying and impractical fallout shelter building). Useful as a production technique to foreground the film's thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary and fictional strands juxtaposed for contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: The docudrama employs juxtaposition (e.g., cutting from scenes of horror to calm lectures or statements by establishment figures) to break the illusion of media-produced 'reality' and highlight the dissonance between official doctrine and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: snippet resembling Herman Kahn followed by scenes of city destruction; bishops' textual statements followed by Canterbury's fate. Juxtaposition is presented as an intentional rhetorical/editorial device to make speakers appear out of touch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternating narrative elements (multiple strands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Features several different strands that alternate: a documentary-style chronology, reportage-like images of the war and its effects, brief contemporary interviews showing public ignorance, optimistic commentary from public figures, and fictional interviews with key figures as the war unfolds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The alternation of these strands is described as central to the film's method of argument and mood-building; evaluators might consider balance and effectiveness of strand transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting preference: amateur and non-actors
rubrics_metrics.description: The cast was almost entirely made up of amateur and non-actors, as was Watkins' preference; casting took place via public meetings and more than 350 actors took part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of amateurs is presented as an intentional stylistic choice to enhance realism; production notes cite locations and casting methods as part of this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on collective portrayal rather than individual focus
rubrics_metrics.description: The film does not focus on individual experiences but rather the collective British population, who rely on government preparations and are not fully convinced of the dangers of nuclear war until the final hours before the attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a thematic/structural criterion: films that foreground social/collective impacts rather than individual arcs are doing a different kind of social critique; assess how effectively collective suffering and social breakdown are rendered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphic, realistic depiction of nuclear effects and aftermath
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed, often graphic depictions of nuclear effects: airbursts, heat waves that melt eyeballs, flash blindness, firestorms, overwhelmed emergency services, mass casualties, radiation sickness, scurvy, mercy killings, executions by police, and long-term illnesses resembling leukaemia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These portrayals are used to argue the plausibility and horror of nuclear war; authenticity and visceral impact (e.g., the firestorm sequence) are cited in later critical praise and can be used as evaluative criteria for effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical analogy and real-world references to support realism
rubrics_metrics.description: The film often invokes historical mass casualty situations (e.g., collection of wedding rings after Dresden, atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki) when portraying a post-attack situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of real historical references is a technique to ground fictional depiction in documented precedent, enhancing persuasive force and perceived realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specific production locations and settings
rubrics_metrics.description: The film was shot in Kent towns (Tonbridge, Gravesend, Chatham, Dover) and much post-strike devastation was shot at Grand Shaft Barracks, Dover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Location choices contribute to verisimilitude and local specificity; production logistics and setting selection are part of film-making criteria for realism and atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial/political constraints on distribution (censorship/withdrawal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The film caused dismay within the BBC and government and was withdrawn before a provisional screening; BBC judged the film 'too horrifying for the medium of broadcasting' and showed it only to invited audiences initially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural/historical fact is both a constraint on release and an indicator of perceived social impact; censorship and delayed broadcast are relevant when assessing the film's historical significance and reception context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reception and acclaim as evaluative metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The film holds a Rotten Tomatoes rating of 93% and won the 1967 Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature. Critics praised its authenticity and horrific portrayal (e.g., Roger Ebert gave a perfect score).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards, critic quotes, and aggregate ratings are presented as measures of the film's importance and effectiveness; they serve as external validation metrics when evaluating the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre classification and thematic labels
rubrics_metrics.description: The article classifies the film as a British pseudo-documentary, mondo film, docudrama, apocalyptic film, Cold War film, anti-nuclear film, survival film and British dystopian film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These genre labels help locate the film within critical and historical categories and suggest different evaluative lenses (documentary authenticity, horror/science-fiction tropes, political/activist films).
